parole.significato: An antechamber, specifically one where visitors wait before being given audience with an influential person such as a p…
parole.testo: From Middle French anticamera and its etymon Italian anticamera, with substitution of ante-, originally after Spanish antecámara, itself after Italian.

parole.significato: Any one of several small coins, circulated around the eastern Mediterranean area from the 12th to 17th centuries.
parole.testo: From Middle English asper, from Middle French aspre or Italian aspro, both from Ancient Greek ἄσπρον (áspron), from neuter of ἄσπρος (áspros, “white”), from Latin asper (“rough, newly minted”).

parole.significato: A short column used in a group to support a rail, as commonly found on the side of a stairway or around a balcony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French balustre, from Italian balaustro (“pillar”), from balausta, balaustio (“wild pomegranate flower”), from Latin balaustium, from Ancient Greek βαλαύστιον (balaústion), from Semitic (compare Classical Syriac ܒܠܳܨܳܐ (blāṣā, “pomegranate shoot”)). Doublet of banister.

parole.significato: An institution where one can place and borrow money and take care of financial affairs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English banke, from Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's bench or table”), from Lombardic bank (“bench, counter”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to turn, curve, be

parole.significato: A large celebratory meal; a feast.
parole.testo: From Middle English banket, from Middle French banquet, from Italian banchetto (“light repast between meals, snack eaten on a small bench”, literally “a small bench”), from banco (“bench”), from Lombardic *bank, *panch (“bench”), from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”). Akin to Old High German bank, b

parole.significato: A marketplace, particularly in the Middle East and South Asia, and often covered with shops and stalls.
parole.testo: From Middle French bazar or Italian bazar, from Ottoman Turkish بازار (bazar), from Persian بازار (bâzâr).

parole.significato: Strong in the face of fear; courageous.
parole.testo: From Middle French brave, borrowed from Italian bravo, itself of uncertain origin (see there). Doublet of bravo.

parole.significato: Being brave, courageousness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French braverie, from braver (“to brave”), or Italian braveria, from bravare (“to brave”). By surface analysis, brave + -ery.

parole.significato: a two-masted vessel, square-rigged on the foremast, but fore-and-aft-rigged mainsail with a square-rig above it on the…
parole.testo: Attested 1525, for a small rowing vessel, from earlier brigandyns, from Middle French brigandin, probably from Italian brigante (“skirmisher, pirate, brigand”), from Latin brigō (“to fight”).

parole.significato: Undyed leather from the skin of buffalo or similar animals.
parole.testo: From buffe (“leather”), from Middle French buffle (“buffalo”).

parole.significato: One who performs in a silly or ridiculous fashion; a clown or fool.
parole.testo: From Middle French bouffon, from Italian buffone (“jester”), from buffare (“to puff out the cheeks”), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Middle High German buffen ("to puff"; > German büffen), Old English pyffan (“to breathe out, blow with the mouth”). More at English puff.

parole.significato: The lowest class of people; the rabble; the vulgar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French canaille.

parole.significato: The firing of artillery for a length of time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French canonnade, a modification of Italian cannonata replacing the suffix -ata with equivalent -ade; by surface analysis, cannon + -ade.

parole.significato: Impulsive and unpredictable; determined by chance, impulse, or whim.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French capricieux, from Italian capriccioso, from capriccio. By surface analysis, caprice + -ious.

parole.significato: A member of an order of Roman Catholic friars.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French capuchin (“Capuchin friar”), from Italian cappuccino (“Capuchin friar”), from cappuccio (“hood, cowl”). Doublet of cappuccino.

parole.significato: A metric unit of mass equal to exactly 200 mg, chiefly used for measuring precious stones and pearls.
parole.testo: From Middle French carat, from Italian carato, from Arabic قِيرَاط (qīrāṭ, “carat, similarly small units such as inches”), from Ancient Greek κεράτιον (kerátion, “hornlet, carob seed”), from κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive suffix). Doublet of quilate and keratin.

parole.significato: Any of a number of festivals held just before the beginning of Lent.
parole.testo: From Middle French carnaval, from Italian carnevale, possibly from the Latin phrase carnem levāmen (“meat dismissal”). Other scholars suggest Latin carnuālia (“meat-based country feast”) or carrus nāvālis (“boat wagon; float”) instead. Doublet of carnaval.

parole.significato: The military arm of service that fights while riding horses.
parole.testo: From Middle French cavalerie, in turn from Italian cavalleria. Recorded in English from the 1540s. Doublet of chivalry.

parole.significato: A scale insect of the species Dactylopius coccus, native to the tropical and subtropical Americas, which lives on prick…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Middle French cochenille (modern French cochenille), from Italian cocciniglia or Spanish cochinilla; further etymology uncertain, possibly from Latin coccineus, coccinus (“scarlet-dyed; scarlet in colour”) (whence Italian coccineo (“scarlet in colour”)) + Italian -iglia (su

parole.significato: A room, or section, or chamber, typically within a vehicle.
parole.testo: First attested 1564, from Middle French compartiment, from Italian compartimento, from Late Latin compartiri (“to divide with, to share with”), from com- + partiri (“to apportion, to divide, to share”).

parole.significato: A female prostitute, especially one with high-status or wealthy clients.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French courtisane, from Italian cortigiana, feminine of cortigiano (“courtier”), from corte (“court”), itself from Latin cohors.

parole.significato: Hair of the head.
parole.testo: From Middle French crine (whence also French crin), Italian crine, or directly from Latin crīnis (“hair of the head, lock of hair, plume”).

parole.significato: Synonym of delicacy.
parole.testo: Apparently from Middle French delicatesse, from delicat (“delicate”) + -esse (“quality”), probably after Italian delicatezza. By surface analysis, delicate + -esse.

parole.significato: An unexpected natural or man-made catastrophe of substantial extent causing significant physical damage or destruction,…
parole.testo: From Middle French desastre, from Italian disastro, from dis- + astro (“star”), from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.

parole.significato: Of the nature of a disaster; calamitous.
parole.testo: From disaster + -ous, after Middle French desastreux (modern French désastreux; from desastre (modern French désastre, “disaster”; from des- + astre, a calque of Italian disastro) + -eux), itself after Italian disastroso, from disastro + -oso, from dis- (“away, without”) (from Latin dis-) + astro (“

parole.significato: A structural element resembling the hollow upper half of a sphere.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dome, domme (modern French dôme), from Italian duomo, from Latin domus (ecclesiae) (literally “house (of the church)”), a calque of Ancient Greek οἶκος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (oîkos tês ekklēsías). Doublet of domus and duomo.

parole.significato: Most-liked. (In other words, [person]'s favorite [noun] = the [noun] that [person] likes the most.)
parole.testo: Attested from the 1580s, borrowed from Middle French favorit, from Old French favorit or Italian favorito (“favoured, favourite”), past participle of Italian favorire (“to favor”), from favore, from Latin favor (“good will, favor”), from the verb faveō (“to favour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Europ

parole.significato: An illustration that is on the page before the title page of a book, a section of one, or a magazine.
parole.testo: From Middle French frontispice, from Italian frontespizio or Medieval Latin frontispicium, from Latin frōns (“forehead”, oblique stem in front-) + -spic- (“to watch”, combining form of speciō) + -ium. Spelling altered due to folk etymology, influenced by piece.

parole.significato: Fashion, style of dressing oneself up.
parole.testo: From Middle French garbe ("graceful outline, silhouette"; > Modern French galbe), from Italian garbo (“grace, elegance”), from Germanic (compare Old High German garwi, garawi (“dress, equipment, preparation”), Middle High German gerwe (“outfitting, jewelry, clothing, robe, regalia”), modern German G

parole.significato: A ruminant in the genus Giraffa of the African savannah with long legs, a highly elongated neck, yellow fur patterned w…
parole.testo: From Middle French giraffe, from Italian giraffa, from Arabic زُرَافَة (zurāfa), from Classical Syriac ܙܪܝܦܐ (zārīp̄ā), from Classical Persian زُرْنَاپَا (zurnāpā, literally “flute-leg”). Displaced camelopard.

parole.significato: Distorted and unnatural in shape or size; abnormal, especially in a hideous way.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French grotesque, from Italian grottesco, from grotta (“cave”) + -esco (relational suffix). By surface analysis, grotto + -esque. Compare French grotesque, English grotto.

parole.significato: A two-handed pole weapon, consisting of a long pole with an axe-like blade mounted on it (at a right angle like an axe,…
parole.testo: (1495) Middle French hallebarde, from Italian alabarda, from Middle High German helmbarte (“broad-axe with handle”), from halm, from Proto-Germanic *helmô (“handle”) + barte (“hatchet”), from *bardaz (“broadax”), literally "beard."

parole.significato: Cheerful and good-humoured; jolly, merry.
parole.testo: First attested in 1590; borrowed from Middle French jovial (“under the influence of Jupiter; of Jove; jovial, jolly”), from Italian gioviale (“(now obsolete) born under the influence of the planet Jupiter”) (attested in Dante, Paradiso, canto XVIII, early 14th century), from Late Latin Ioviālis (“re

parole.significato: To form an association; to unite in a league or confederacy; to combine for mutual support.
parole.testo: From Middle English liege, ligg, lige (“a pact between governments, an agreement, alliance”), from Middle French ligue, from Italian lega, from the verb legare, from Latin ligō (“to tie”).

parole.significato: The act of exchange of an asset of lesser liquidity with a more liquid one, such as cash.
parole.testo: * From liquidate + -ion (suffix forming nouns denoting an action or process). Liquidate is a learned borrowing from Late Latin liquidātus, the perfect passive participle of liquidō (“to turn into a liquid, melt; to make clear”), from Classical Latin liquidus (“fluid, liquid; clear, transparent”) + -

parole.significato: A nonacademic, periodical publication which consists of articles by multiple writers on some broad topic or theme.
parole.testo: From Middle English magasyne, from Middle French magasin (“warehouse, store”), from Italian magazzino (“storehouse”), ultimately from Arabic مَخَازِن pl (maḵāzin), plural of مَخْزَن (maḵzan, “storeroom, storehouse”), noun of place from خَزَنَ (ḵazana, “to store, to stock, to lay up”). First attested

parole.significato: The territory held by a marquis, margrave or marchioness.
parole.testo: From marquis + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it), on the pattern of Middle French marquisat, Italian marchesato.

parole.significato: A cover, or partial cover, for the face, used for disguise or protection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French masque (“a covering to hide or protect the face”), from Italian maschera (“mask, disguise”), from (a byform of, see it for more) Medieval Latin masca, mascha, a borrowing of Proto-West Germanic *maskā, from which English mesh and mask (“mesh”) (below at Etymology 2) are i

parole.significato: An assembly or party of people wearing (usually elaborate or fanciful) masks and costumes, and amusing themselves with…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Middle French mascarade, masquarade, masquerade (modern French mascarade (“masquerade, masque; farce”)), and its etymon Italian mascherata (“masquerade”), from maschera (“mask”) + -ata. Maschera is derived from Medieval Latin masca (“mask”): see further there. The English w

parole.significato: A stamped metal disc used as a personal ornament, a charm, or a religious object.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French medaille, medale, from Italian medaglia (originally "half a denarius"), from Early Medieval Latin medālia, feminine derived via dissimilation (/dj–lj/ > /d–lj/) from mediālia, neuter plural of Late Latin mediālis (“middle”, adjective), from Classical L

parole.significato: The cardinal number 1 000 000: 10⁶; a thousand thousand (1,000²).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English milioun, from Middle French milion, from Old French millon, from Italian milione (“million”, from mille (“thousand”, from Latin mille) + -one). Compare -illion.

parole.significato: Yarn or fabric made from the hair of the angora goat, often as mixed with cotton or other materials.
parole.testo: Earlier mocayre, from Middle French mocayart and Italian mocaiardo, mocaiarro, both from Arabic مُخَيَّر (muḵayyar, “choice”), past participle of خَيَّرَ (ḵayyara, “to choose”). Form influenced by hair through folk etymology. Doublet of moire; compare mockado.

parole.significato: A piece of artwork created by placing colored pieces (usually tiles, either regular or irregular in shape) in a pattern…
parole.testo: From Middle French mosaïque, from Italian mosaico, from Medieval Latin musaicum, from Late Latin musivum (opus), from Latin museum, musaeum, probably from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)). Doublet of museum.

parole.significato: A place of worship for Muslims, often having at least one minaret; a masjid.
parole.testo: From Middle French mosquée, from Italian moschea, ultimately from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, literally “place of prostration”). Doublet of masjid.

parole.significato: A growth of facial hair between the nose and the upper lip.
parole.testo: Used in English since the 16th century. From Middle French moustache from Italian mostaccio, from Early Medieval Latin mustācium, from Byzantine Greek μουστάκιον (moustákion), diminutive of (Doric) Ancient Greek μύσταξ (mústax, “upper lip”), of unknown origin (probably a Pre-Greek substrate). Replac

parole.significato: An evergreen tree of the genus Citrus such as Citrus sinensis which yields oranges (the fruit).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English orenge, orange, from Old French pome orenge (“fruit orange”), influenced by the place name Orange (which is from Gaulish and unrelated to the word for the fruit and colour) and by Old Occitan auranja and calqued from Old Italian melarancio, melarancia, compound of mela

parole.significato: Any of several large, ferocious sea creatures, now especially the killer whale.
parole.testo: From Middle French orque, Italian orca, and their source, Latin orca (“type of whale”). Doublet of orca.

parole.significato: A member of the Ottoman dynasty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Ottoman (“Osman”), borrowed from Italian Ottomano, borrowed from Arabic عُثْمَان (ʕuṯmān). Doublet of Osman and Uthman.

parole.significato: A large wild feline, such as a lynx or cougar.
parole.testo: From Middle French once, from Old French lonce (“lynx”), by false division (the l was thought to be the article), from Italian lonza, ultimately from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx, “lynx”). Doublet of onza and lynx.

parole.significato: A 17th-century game in which a ball was driven along an alley and through a hoop using a mallet.
parole.testo: From Middle French pallemaille, pale-maille, from Italian pallamaglio (“ball-hammer”), from Italian palla (“ball”) and maglio (“hammer”).

parole.significato: A low protective wall.
parole.testo: From Middle French parapet, from Italian parapetto.

parole.significato: A lampoon, originally as published in public; a satire or libel on someone.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Italian pasquinata, from Pasquino, name given to a statue in Rome on which lampoons were posted.

parole.significato: A person who makes an excessive or tedious show of their knowledge, especially regarding rules of vocabulary and gramma…
parole.testo: From Middle French pedant, pedante, from Italian pedante (“a teacher, schoolmaster, pedant”), associated with unrelated Italian pedagogo (“teacher, pedagogue”). Compare French pédant.

parole.significato: The base or foot of a column, statue, vase, lamp.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French piédestal, itself borrowed from Italian piedistallo (literally “foot stand”). Spelling influenced by Latin pēs, pedem.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Persia.
parole.testo: From Middle English Persien, from Middle French persien, from Italian persiano, from Medieval Latin Persiānus, from Persia (itself from Persēs/Persa (“Persian man”) [from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs), itself from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠Pārsa⁠/, “Persian”)] + -ia (suffix forming country names))

parole.significato: A rectangular column that projects partially from the wall to which it is attached; it gives the appearance of a suppor…
parole.testo: From Middle French pilastre, from Italian pilastro. Equivalent to pillar + -aster.

parole.significato: A person who steers a ship, a helmsman.
parole.testo: From Middle French pilot, pillot, from Italian pilota, piloto, older also pedotta, pedot(t)o (the form in pil- is probably influenced by pileggiare (“to sail, navigate”)); ultimately from unattested Byzantine Greek *πηδώτης (*pēdṓtēs, “helmsman”), from Ancient Greek πηδόν (pēdón, “blade of an oar, o

parole.significato: A contract of insurance.
parole.testo: From Middle French police, from Italian polizza, from Medieval Latin apodissa (“receipt for money”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis, “proof, declaration”). Doublet of apodixis.

parole.significato: An ignoble or total coward; a dastard; a mean-spirited wretch.
parole.testo: From Middle French poltron, from Italian poltrone.

parole.significato: The common people of a nation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French populace, from Italian popolaccio, from popolo + -accio (“pejorative suffix”), from Latin populus.

parole.significato: Each of a series of men stationed at specific places along a postroad, with responsibility for relaying letters and dis…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French poste, from Italian posta (“stopping-place for coaches”), feminine of posto (“placed, situated”).

parole.significato: A rider mounted on the near (left) leading horse who guides the team pulling a carriage.
parole.testo: From Middle French postillon, and its likely source, Italian postiglione (“guide for driver of post-coach”), from posta (“post”).

parole.significato: The way a person holds and positions their body.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French posture, from Italian postura, from Latin positūra (“position, situation”). Doublet of positura.

parole.significato: Pumpkin.
parole.testo: From Middle French pompon (“melon, cucumber”), from Italian popone (“melon”) (chiefly Tuscan dialect), from Latin pepō, peponis (“large melon”). Doublet of pepo.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A group of sentient beings, particularly people, distinguished by common ancestry, heritage or characteristics (see Wik…
parole.testo: 1560s, via Middle French race from Italian razza (early 14th century), of uncertain origin. Partially displaced native Middle English kinde (“kind, type, sort, race, nature”), whence English kind. Fully displaced native Old English cnōsl and hād. theories * Diez and some other scholars suggest deriv

parole.significato: To compensate (someone) with payment; especially, to repay money spent on someone's behalf.
parole.testo: 1591, re- (“back”) + imburse (“pay”, literally “put in a purse”) (perhaps after Middle French rembourser or Italian rimborsàre), from Middle French embourser, from Old French en- (“in”) + borser (“to get money”), from borse (“purse”), from Medieval Latin bursa (English purse).

parole.significato: A scoundrel, rascal, or unprincipled, deceitful, brutal and unreliable person.
parole.testo: From Middle French rufian, from Italian ruffiano (“pimp”).

parole.significato: A sword of Persian origin that features a curved blade.
parole.testo: First attested in 1548. From Middle French cimeterre (15c.) or directly from Italian scimitarra, possibly from an unknown Ottoman Turkish word, ultimately from Classical Persian شمشیر (šamšēr, “sword”). Doublet of shamshir.

parole.significato: A seraglio.
parole.testo: From Middle French sérail, from Italian serraglio.

parole.significato: salary; military pay
parole.testo: From Middle English solde, sould, soud, from Middle French solde, Italian soldo. Compare soldier and Danish sold (via Low German). Doublet of sol, soldo, solid, solidus, sou, and xu.

parole.significato: A fixed verse form of Italian origin consisting of fourteen lines that are typically five-foot iambics and rhyme accord…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sonnet, from Italian sonetto, from Old Occitan sonet (“a song”), diminutive of son (“song, sound”), from Latin sonus (“sound”).

parole.significato: Frozen fruit juice, sometimes mixed with egg whites, eaten as dessert or between courses of a meal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sorbet, borrowed from Italian sorbetto, borrowed from Ottoman Turkish شربت (şerbet), borrowed from Classical Persian شَرْبَت (šarbat), borrowed from Arabic شَرْبَة (šarba), from شَرِبَ (šariba). Doublet of sherbet and sharbat, related to syrup.

parole.significato: A pointed weapon similar to a pike.
parole.testo: From Middle French sponton (also esponton), from Italian spontone, from spunta (“pike”).

parole.significato: Foul play; an attack made by deceit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French supercherie, itself borrowed from Italian soperchieria.

parole.significato: The empty weight of a container; unladen weight.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tare, from Italian tara, from Arabic طَرْحَة (ṭarḥa, “that which is thrown away”), a derivative of طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “to throw (away)”).

parole.significato: Moving pedestrians or vehicles, or the flux or passage thereof.
parole.testo: From Middle French trafique, traffique (“traffic”), from Italian traffico (“traffic”) from trafficare (“to carry on trade”). Potentially from Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcāre (“to rub across”); Klein instead suggests the Italian has ultimate origin in Arabic تَفْرِيق (tafrīq, “distribution, dispersion”),

parole.significato: The genre of drama that combines elements of tragedy and comedy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tragicomédie (whence French tragicomédie), itself borrowed from Italian tragicommedia, from Latin tragicōmoedia, tragicocōmoedia. By surface analysis, tragic + comedy, with haplology.

parole.significato: A man's headdress made by winding a length of cloth round the head.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French turbant, from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband), also the root of tulip.

parole.significato: To jump or leap over with a hand and/or foot on the item for support.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French volter (“to turn or spin around; to frolic”), borrowed from Italian voltare, itself from a Vulgar Latin frequentative form of Latin volvere; later assimilated to Etymology 1, above.

parole.significato: Unusual and awkward in a funny, comical manner; outlandish; clownish.
parole.testo: From Middle French zani, zanni, from Italian zanni (“a kind of masked clown character”), from Zanni, a Venetian form of Giovanni. Doublet of Zanni, John, and Giovanni.
